paper_a.title: On the Multilinear Restriction and Kakeya conjectures

paper_b.title: The endpoint case of the Bennett-Carbery-Tao multilinear Kakeya conjecture

metadata.description: Bennett-Carbery-Tao (paper A) prove the multilinear Kakeya inequality with arbitrarily small $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss at the endpoint exponent $q=d/(d-1)$ via a heat-flow / monotonicity argument generalising Loomis-Whitney. Guth (paper B) closes the endpoint by removing the $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss and obtaining sharp $\theta$-dependence, using an entirely different polynomial-method machinery (polynomial ham sandwich + Lusternik-Schnirelmann visibility). Paper B thus extends paper A's main theorem (Conjecture MLKC / Theorem kakthm) to the sharp endpoint, while overlap of intermediate machinery is minimal: only the underlying objects (transversal $\delta$-tubes / cylinders) and the cited Loomis-Whitney inequality are shared.

matches.explanation: Paper A's Multilinear Kakeya Conjecture at the endpoint $q=d/(d-1)$ is exactly the inequality Guth proves as Theorem 2 (the multilinear Kakeya endpoint estimate). Both state the same bound $\|\prod_j \sum_{T_j} \chi_{T_j}\|_{L^{1/(d-1)}} \leq C \theta^{-1/(d-1)} \prod_j (\#\T_j)^{1/(d-1)}$ for $d$-tuples of transversal cylinders/$\delta$-tubes, which is the central conjecture in paper A and the main result in paper B. Guth's theorem makes the constant's dependence on the transversality $\theta$ explicit.

Paper A's Theorem kakthm (`Near-optimal multilinear Kakeya') proves the multilinear Kakeya bound for $q > d/(d-1)$ and obtains an $\eps$-loss endpoint $\|\cdot\|_{L^{1/(d-1)}} \leq C\delta^{-\eps}\prod_j(\delta^{d-1}\#\T_j)$. Paper B's Theorem 2 (TP405.1) is the genuine endpoint statement with NO $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss and explicit $\theta^{-1/(d-1)}$ constant. Same inequality, sharper bound — this is the EXT signal: B strictly extends A at the endpoint.

Paper A's $n$-linear Kakeya in $\R^d$ (TP404.4) handles the multilinear Kakeya inequality for $n \leq d$ tubes in $\R^d$ with $\delta^{-\eps}$ loss. Paper B's main theorem is stated for the diagonal case $n=d$ but its method readily yields the more general $n$-linear setting. Same family of inequalities, A is more general in $(n,d)$ but with $\eps$-loss, B is sharper but stated for $n=d$.

Both papers cite the classical Loomis-Whitney inequality (1949) as external prior work in the same role: the axis-parallel limit of the multilinear Kakeya inequality. Paper A states the integrated form $\int \prod f_j(\pi_j(x)) \leq \prod \|f_j\|_{d-1}$; Paper B states the volume corollary $Vol(U) \leq B^{n/(n-1)}$. Both are the same theorem; this match carries no signal about the A-vs-B relationship.

Both papers contain the same observation as a remark: in the axis-parallel/linear $\Sigma_j$ limit, the multilinear Kakeya inequality reduces to the classical Loomis-Whitney inequality. Paper A's RP404.2 phrases it via Plancherel; Paper B's RP405.2 phrases it via projections $\pi_j(I)$. Same conceptual content.

Paper A defines $\delta$-tubes (DP404.4) — rectangular boxes of dimensions $\delta \times\cdots\times\delta\times 1$ — and transversal families thereof (DP404.5). Paper B defines unit cylinders (DP405.1) of radius $R$ around a line. After scaling (cylinders have radius 1 instead of $\delta$, length $\sim$ ambient scale), these are the same geometric object; A's family parametrises tubes by orientation, while B's tubes are unscaled cylinders. The transversality condition in A's DP404.5 (orientations near $e_j$) plays the same role as the angle $(100n)^{-1}$ assumption in TP405.2 / B's quantitative determinant condition $|\det(v_{1,a_1},\ldots,v_{n,a_n})|\geq\theta$ in TP405.1.

Paper A's transversality (spanning) condition (DP404.2) is stated for smooth submanifold parametrisations $\Sigma_j$ — a continuous, $C^2$-smoothness-coupled hypothesis used in the multilinear restriction setting. Paper B has no analogue at this level of generality; B only treats straight cylinders, where transversality reduces to the determinant condition embedded in TP405.1's hypothesis. Listed for completeness because A's spanning condition is a paper-origin contribution.

Paper A's $C^2$-smoothness condition on $\Sigma_j$ (DP404.3) has no counterpart in B: Guth treats only straight cylinders, so smoothness is automatic and the assumption does not appear. Specific to A's restriction-side machinery.

The extension operator $\ex g(\xi) = \int g(x) e^{i\xi\cdot\Sigma(x)} dx$ (DP404.1) is the central object of A's restriction-conjecture half. Paper B does not treat the restriction conjecture and has no extension operator.
The Loomis-Whitney matrix $A_j^0$ (orthogonal projection onto $\{x_j=0\}$) is part of A's algebraic monotonicity machinery. B's polynomial-method proof has no matrix-based formulation.
Positive semi-definite ordering $A\leq_{pd} B$ is a tool used in A's heat-flow monotonicity arguments (PrP404.2, PrP404.3, LP404.3). No analogue in B.

The sliding gaussian quantity $f_j(t,x)$ and the monotone quantity $Q_p(t)$ are A's heat-flow / Bellman-type monotonicity gadgets — the technical heart of A's proof of the multilinear Kakeya inequality. They are entirely absent from B's polynomial method.

Joints (DP404.10) and $\theta$-transverse joints (DP404.11) are A-specific definitions for A's joints estimate (TP404.7), an application of the multilinear Kakeya theorem. B's paper does not address joints.
Variable-coefficient operator $S_\lambda$ and curvy tube $T_j$ are A-specific objects for A's variable-coefficient extension (TP404.5, TP404.6). B treats only straight cylinders.

The $\re^*$ / $\ka^*$ schemata are A's notational shorthand for parametric families of multilinear restriction / Kakeya estimates with prescribed loss exponent $\alpha$. B does not parametrise its inequalities this way.
Linear Restriction Conjecture is A's restriction-side conjecture; B does not treat the restriction problem at all.
Multilinear Restriction Conjecture (CnjP404.2) is A's other main conjecture, proved with $R^\eps$ loss as TP404.3. B's polynomial method does not address restriction.
Linear Kakeya Conjecture (the original Kakeya conjecture for $\delta$-separated tubes) is mentioned in A as motivation. B addresses only multilinear Kakeya.
A's near-optimal multilinear restriction theorem with $R^\eps$ loss is the restriction-side analogue of TP404.2. B does not treat restriction.

Variable-coefficient (curvy) versions of multilinear restriction and Kakeya. B treats only the constant-coefficient (straight-tube) case, so A's variable-coefficient extensions are A-original contributions absent from B.

A's joints estimate ($n^{3/2+\eps}$ count of $\theta$-transverse joints in $\R^3$) is an application of multilinear Kakeya specific to A. Notably, B's polynomial method later inspired Guth-Katz's sharp joints theorem in subsequent work, but in this paper B does not address joints directly.

A's bootstrap proposition $\re^* + \ka^* \Rightarrow$ improved $\re^*$ is A's mechanism for transferring multilinear Kakeya into multilinear restriction. B has no such bootstrap — its proof of multilinear Kakeya is direct via polynomial method.

Loomis-Whitney monotonicity proposition — A's central technical innovation. The heat-flow / sliding-gaussian monotonicity has no counterpart whatsoever in B; this is the principal methodological gap that makes A and B 'competing approaches' to the same conjecture, ultimately tagged EXT because B is sharper.
Approximate (perturbed) Loomis-Whitney monotonicity — A's quantitative perturbation of PrP404.2 used to prove the actual Theorem kakthm. Tied entirely to A's heat-flow approach.
A's negative result ($Q_p$ can fail to be monotone at the endpoint unless $W_j$ are singletons) is internal commentary on the limitations of the heat-flow method. No B-side analogue.
Curvy Kakeya / curvy restriction bootstrap propositions are A's variable-coefficient bootstrapping. B treats only straight cylinders.
Uncertainty principle for $\re^*$ — auxiliary lemma in A's restriction-Kakeya equivalence. No restriction analogue in B.
Closed-form formula for the symbol $S$ at $\B_j = M_j^{1/2}$ — algebraic lemma internal to A's heat-flow proof. No B-side analogue.
Rigidity of rank-$(d-1)$ Loomis-Whitney configurations — algebraic lemma underpinning A's perturbation analysis (used in PrP404.4).
Polynomial extrapolation in $p$ (Appendix lemma) — technical device for A's heat-flow argument allowing extension from $p\in\N^n$ to $p\in(0,\infty)^n$. No B-side analogue.
Loomis-Whitney bound at $t=1$ and its perturbed version are corollaries of the heat-flow monotonicity argument; tied to A's specific approach.

The endpoint $L^2$ multilinear restriction equation $\|\prod \ex_j g_j\|_{L^{2/(d-1)}} \leq C\prod\|g_j\|_2$ and the reduction of MLRC to this endpoint are restriction-side. B does not treat restriction.
Loomis-Whitney gaussian reformulation — A's heat-flow recasting of Loomis-Whitney. No B-side analogue.
Internal formulas for $G(p,t,x)$ and the choice of $v_0$ killing the bad term — all internal to A's heat-flow proof of PrP404.3.
Brascamp-Lieb connection — remark linking A's monotonicity to Lieb's gaussian-exhaustion theorem. No B-side analogue (B is independent of Brascamp-Lieb).
A speculates that variants of its techniques may attack the linear Kakeya conjecture; B does not pursue linear Kakeya. Treated as none.

Directed volume $V_S(v) = \int_S |v\cdot N| \, dvol_S$ is the central B-side object measuring how well a hypersurface intercepts a direction. A has no notion of directed volume on a hypersurface; A's machinery uses gaussian weights instead.
Visibility, mollified directed volume, and mollified visibility are B's polynomial-method invariants. A has no polynomial / cohomology framework, so these have no A-side counterpart.

Bisection set $Bi(U_1,\dots,U_r)$ in $\mathbb{RP}^N$ — projective parameter space of bisecting algebraic hypersurfaces. Fundamental to B's polynomial ham sandwich + Lusternik-Schnirelmann strategy. No A-side analogue.
The metric on the space of ellipsoids is auxiliary B-machinery used in B's visibility lemma. No A-side analogue.

B's Theorem 1 (axis-aligned multilinear Kakeya volume bound, $Vol(I) \leq C(n) A^{n/(n-1)}$) is an axis-aligned simplification proved first in B via polynomial method as warm-up. A does not state a corresponding axis-aligned volume version separately; A's general theorem (TP404.2) implies it but is broader. Tagged none because the specific axis-aligned $L^\infty$-flavoured statement is original to B.
Lusternik-Schnirelmann vanishing lemma — algebraic-topology lemma central to B. Has no A-side analogue (A uses no cohomology).

Cylinder estimate (LP405.2) and Volume vs. directed-volume sum (LP405.3) — geometric lemmas tying the directed volume of a degree-$d$ hypersurface inside a cylinder to $r^{n-1} d$. Both depend on B's directed-volume machinery, which has no A-side counterpart.
Continuity Lemma and Basic Area Estimate are B-original technical lemmas for the polynomial ham sandwich theorem and bisection arguments.
Bisection Lemma and Multiple Bisection Lemma — B-original cohomological reformulations of the polynomial ham sandwich theorem. No A-side analogues.

B's visibility-lemma chain (mollified properties, Visibility Lemma, Weak Visibility Lemma, directed-volume-on-bisecting-ellipsoids, Large Visibility on Many Cubes) is the technical heart of B's polynomial method. Entirely absent from A.

Visibility-vs-directional-volume product (Lemma 6.1) and average directional volume along a tube (Lemma 7.1) — the final assembly lemmas in B's proof of the endpoint multilinear Kakeya estimate. Internal to B's polynomial method.

B's Box Estimate (`planiness for unions of tubes') — proposition exhibiting that a union of cylinders has a low-volume convex body $B(x)$ at typical points $x$, controlling tube escape probabilities. This is a downstream application of B's visibility machinery, with no A-side counterpart.
Directed volume formula via projection (EP405.1) and the discrete-sum reduction $\sum_k F(Q_k)^{1/(n-1)}$ (EP405.2) are B-internal equations specific to the polynomial-method proof.
Proof of A's restriction $\Leftrightarrow$ Kakeya proposition via uncertainty principle. Restriction-side, no B analogue.
Proofs of Loomis-Whitney monotonicity (PP404.2) and approximate monotonicity (PP404.3) — the heart of A's heat-flow approach. Wholly distinct from B's proof of the same multilinear Kakeya inequality.

Both proofs target (a sibling of) the multilinear Kakeya inequality but via dramatically different routes: PP404.2 (heat-flow monotonicity of $Q_p(t)$, completing the square, probabilistic reformulation, polynomial extrapolation in $p$) versus PP405.16 (polynomial ham sandwich to find $Z$ with calibrated visibility, cylinder estimate plus Holder chain). Aligned at the proof level because they prove the same / a refined version of the central inequality, but structurally and methodologically disjoint. Listed as a proof-level analogue at confidence medium to record the EXT/AP boundary case.
Proof of joints theorem in $\R^3$ — A-specific application.
Proofs of A's auxiliary lemmas (rank rigidity, curvy bootstrap variants, formula for $S$, polynomial extrapolation). All A-specific to the heat-flow / restriction machinery.
Lattice-grid lower bound for joints (~$n^{3/2}$ joints) — example specific to A's joints theorem. (Auxiliary, listed for completeness even though `none` matches on examples are not required.)
Examples illustrating B's directed volume / visibility on disks. Specific to B's machinery; no A-side analogue. (Auxiliary; listed sparingly.)
Remark that B's Theorem 2 generalizes B's Theorem 1 (within B). Internal to B.
Why-mollify and why-include-$|v|\leq 1$ remarks — B-internal motivation for design choices in the visibility definition. No A-side analogue (A has no visibility).
